title: Bhong Mosque: a modern work of many crafts
summary: Bhong Mosque is a twentieth-century work of collective craftsmanship. Its architectural importance lies in the inventive meeting of materials, references and skilled labour.

body.text: Bhong Mosque can look older than it is to a viewer who equates dense ornament with a distant past. It is, instead, a major twentieth-century architectural project. Work began in 1932 under Rais Ghazi Mohammad, and the Aga Khan Award for Architecture records completion in 1982. Its recognition in the 1986 award cycle makes it part of the history of modern architecture as well as the history of mosque building.

The award record credits local master masons and craftsmen rather than a single professional architect. It describes specialists drawn from several places, including Rajasthan and Karachi. This is an important starting point. The building emerged from coordinated skills developed over decades, not simply from a finished design translated mechanically into stone and plaster.
Many materials, one demanding composition

The project brought together carving, inlay, tilework, mirror work, painting and calligraphy. The wider compound also employed industrially produced materials alongside traditional ones. The award account distinguishes these from the traditional materials of the mosque interior. That distinction helps explain why the building should not be reduced to either an untouched craft tradition or a modern imitation of an older style.

A study of its ornamentation discusses the involvement of skilled workers and their apprentices. Such a working relationship makes craft transmission part of the architectural story. A finished pattern is the visible outcome; the ability to set it out, cut it, fit it and repair it is another form of knowledge. The latter is less easily photographed but equally important.

The mosque’s intensity can initially make individual decisions hard to see. One useful approach is to follow a single material across a surface. Where does tile give way to paint? Where does reflective work concentrate light? How does a calligraphic band establish a boundary? These questions reveal organisation within abundance, rather than treating ornament as an undifferentiated covering.
Modern does not have to mean unadorned

Bhong challenges a narrow definition of modern architecture as necessarily plain, industrial or detached from inherited forms. Its eclectic references were part of the award discussion, not an embarrassment concealed behind the prize. The building asks whether invention can occur through combination and elaboration as well as through reduction.

That does not require every viewer to find the composition harmonious. A considered response can acknowledge tension, density and differences of taste. Architectural significance is not the same as universal agreement about beauty. The mosque provides a particularly clear opportunity to discuss that distinction without dismissing the makers or the community for whom it was built.

For an archive, the best presentation would pair an overall view with a small number of carefully explained details. Each detail should identify its material and position rather than simply celebrate intricacy. Bhong’s achievement becomes more legible when the work of making is visible: a sustained collaboration in which contemporary patronage, inherited skills and new materials all had a part.

title: Harrand Fort and the southern Punjab frontier
summary: Harrand Fort’s enclosure and gateways are firmer evidence than its many origin stories. Reading the surviving structure reveals a frontier place with several historical lives.

body.text: Harrand Fort is a place where the surviving enclosure offers a more reliable beginning than the most dramatic story about its origins. The official archaeological catalogue describes an approximately circular fort built with small bricks and mud mortar, strengthened by repeated bastions and entered from the east and west. These are concrete features that can be examined, measured and compared.

The Rajanpur district administration presents a much longer historical narrative, but also admits uncertainty about the fort’s foundation. Its page combines early legends with accounts of Sikh rebuilding and later British military use; elsewhere on the same page it labels the fort British-period. These statements do not establish a single construction date. They demonstrate why the age of a place and the date of its surviving masonry must be treated as separate questions.
Following the enclosure

The catalogue records sixteen bastions, with octagonal forms. Their repetition gives the perimeter a recognisable rhythm. On a plan, the relationship between bastion and connecting wall would be more informative than the number alone. It would show how the enclosure responds to its ground and how the entrances interrupt the defensive line.

An east–west pair of gateways also raises questions about movement. Were both used in the same way? How did internal paths connect them? Which buildings stood close to the entrances? The surviving arrangement can guide those questions, but an answer requires more than assuming that every fort followed an identical military plan.

Brick size and mortar are another part of the evidence. A change in either may indicate a repair or a separate construction episode, although it does not automatically supply a date. Recording such changes would be particularly valuable at a place with a long reputation for repeated occupation. A neat dynasty-by-dynasty narrative can otherwise hide the very evidence that might test it.
A frontier history without invented certainty

The district account places Harrand within a history of military posts and changing control. Its regional setting makes routes, settlement and terrain appropriate subjects for further study. Yet a line drawn on a modern map cannot prove the itinerary of an ancient army. Nor can a coin reportedly found somewhere in a fort establish the date of the entire enclosure without a documented context.

This is not an argument for ignoring local traditions. They can reveal how people have understood Harrand and connected it to larger histories. They should be identified as traditions, with the storyteller and circumstances recorded where possible, rather than converted into anonymous facts.

Harrand’s strongest public story brings these forms of evidence into dialogue. The walls show a built defensive place; administrative accounts record later military uses; oral narratives give it a longer remembered past. Keeping those strands distinct allows the fort to remain historically rich without claiming that its most uncertain chapters have already been solved. Current access and custodianship should be confirmed locally before any visit.

title: Haveli Sujan Singh: the courtyard as an urban refuge
summary: Sujan Singh Haveli’s courtyard and sequence of thresholds reveal an urban house beyond its ornate doorway. Its changing surroundings are part of the architectural story.

body.text: Sujan Singh Haveli is often encountered through its ornate entrance, but the doorway is only the beginning of its architecture. The house is organised around an open courtyard, reached through a sequence of entrance spaces. That movement from street to interior is central to its character. A facade photograph can celebrate workmanship while leaving the actual experience of the building almost unexplained.

The archaeological catalogue describes a recessed entrance porch, a substantial main door and routes leading toward the courtyard. Rooms flank parts of the court, while a larger hall occupies another side. Stairs connect levels. Rather than treating these as a list of components, imagine them as a series of choices about access, visibility and the relationship between shared and enclosed spaces.
The courtyard as an organising space

An open court gives a house an interior centre that is not itself a room. Doors and verandas can address it, and changes in light can make its edges more prominent than its middle. In reading Sujan Singh Haveli, the useful question is not simply whether the courtyard is attractive. It is how the surrounding spaces depend on it to form a coherent domestic arrangement.

The idea of an urban refuge is therefore architectural rather than a claim that the house was always secluded or silent. A threshold can delay a view; a change of direction can separate an entrance from a principal space. These effects can be investigated from a plan and photographs without inventing the household’s daily routines.

The catalogue’s description also recalls a former garden setting and a more dispersed surrounding landscape. That reminder complicates the present association with dense Rawalpindi streets. A building does not retain the same urban meaning when its surroundings change. Its former relationship to open ground deserves to be studied alongside its later place in the city.
Repairing a house, not just a front

Reports of conservation activity provide another layer. The National College of Arts’ involvement was reported in 2015, and an official statement carried by APP in 2021 described a restoration planning exercise. The latter noted surviving doors, iron elements and tiles. These are dated accounts of work and intentions, not evidence that every proposed intervention has since been completed.

They nevertheless identify an important principle: the building’s character rests in a combination of materials. Replacing a door, altering a roof or removing a floor finish can change more than a decorative detail. Each may affect the way rooms connect and the way the interior is understood.

An archive presentation should therefore follow the house inward. Begin at the street, pass through the entrance, establish the courtyard and then examine selected details in their positions. That sequence makes the haveli legible as a place of habitation and changing urban circumstances. It also gives its craftsmanship a purpose beyond the production of an impressive image.

title: Khem Singh Bedi Haveli: painted rooms and public memory
summary: The painted rooms of Khem Singh Bedi Haveli bring architectural space and religious imagery together. Their interpretation requires care about both subject matter and changing condition.

body.text: Khem Singh Bedi Haveli at Kallar Syedan is distinguished by painted surfaces that belong to an architectural setting, not a detached gallery collection. The archaeological catalogue records frescoes across the facade, veranda pillars and interior rooms. It also describes courtyards, projecting windows and several levels. The paintings and the spaces that hold them need to be read together.

The house is associated with Khem Singh Bedi, the nineteenth-century Sikh religious and social figure. In a 2021 study, art historian Muhammad Asghar examined its paintings through field research and the interpretation of religious imagery. His published abstract identifies subjects connected with Sikh, Hindu and Islamic traditions. That is a more useful starting point than assuming that a house associated with one community contains only one visual tradition.
Images in domestic space

The position of a painting affects how it is encountered. A figure above an opening is seen differently from one at eye level, and a sequence across a veranda differs from an isolated panel in an enclosed room. An adequate record should therefore include the wall, the opening and the surrounding decoration, not only a tightly cropped figure.

Asghar interprets the imagery in terms of cultural syncretism and the patron’s religious outlook. That interpretation should be attributed to the researcher. It is not the same as a surviving statement by the patron explaining every painted subject. The distinction allows an engaging argument to remain open to discussion rather than hardening into a claim about someone’s private intentions.

Individual identifications also require care. Clothing, attributes, inscriptions and comparison may support a reading, but a confident social-media caption is not sufficient evidence. Where a figure has not been securely identified, describing what is visible can be more honest and more useful than naming a deity or ruler prematurely.
A record of condition has a date

The catalogue’s positive description of the paintings’ condition cannot be treated as a timeless assessment. The 2021 study’s abstract, by contrast, expresses concern about deterioration. These sources belong to different moments and may have assessed different aspects of the building. Their contrast is a reason to seek dated photographs and surveys, not to choose whichever description produces the more dramatic story.

Documentation can preserve information about a painting without physically preserving the painting itself. Both are needed. A photograph records a surface at one moment; conservation requires an understanding of the material, its support and the causes of change. Digital colour correction should not be mistaken for recovery of the original scheme.

The haveli’s public value lies partly in this encounter between image, room and historical interpretation. Its paintings offer evidence of a varied visual world, while its architecture shows how that world was placed within a home. Keeping the two together gives the site a depth that the label colourful mansion cannot convey, and makes careful, contextual recording an essential part of its future.

title: Historic Bhera beyond a single gate
summary: Bhera’s heritage is an urban network of gates, streets and reused buildings. Understanding that network is more useful than reducing the town to one landmark or a disputed gate count.

body.text: Bhera is best understood as an urban ensemble rather than a collection of unrelated monuments. Gates, streets, houses and religious buildings form a network, and the meaning of any one element depends partly on the others. A gate photographed without the street behind it becomes a facade. Seen in its urban setting, it is also an entrance, a route marker and a point where the town’s edges have changed.

The Department of Archaeology and Museums places Bhera on the left bank of the Jhelum and describes its association with routes toward Lahore and Multan. Its account also notes substantial rebuilding of gates in the nineteenth century. That matters because the historical foundation of a walled town cannot be used as the date of every structure visible there today.
Why counting gates is not enough

Different inventories do not always count the same things. The national catalogue refers to eight gates, while the Urban Unit’s 2022 heritage plan lists nine, including an Inner Lahore Gate. The difference should be explained through the scope and naming of each inventory rather than silently converted into a single unquestioned total. An inner gateway and an outer entrance may belong to different levels of an urban system.

The Urban Unit records several nineteenth-century dates and distinguishes surviving, altered and lost gateways. Those categories are more informative than a simple checklist. A missing gate can remain significant in a street name or route, while a standing gate may contain substantial later work. Neither is adequately described by the binary labels original and destroyed.

The same report records a former gurdwara used as an imambargah, with local testimony about its condition around Partition. This is evidence of changing use, not permission to assume that every feature belongs to the building’s first function. The account should retain the difference between the physical record and what a caretaker recalled hearing from earlier generations.
The city between the monuments

Urban heritage includes the connections between celebrated buildings. Street width, the alignment of an entrance and the scale of adjoining construction influence how a place is experienced. A conservation project focused only on isolated fronts can miss these relationships. Equally, a plan that treats present residents and businesses as visual clutter misses the fact that the town continues to function.

Punjab’s 2025–26 tourism programme listed an unapproved proposal for heritage conservation in Bhera. That planning record signals institutional interest, but it does not establish a completed transformation. Any account of subsequent work needs its own dated evidence.

For an archive or a careful walk, Bhera suggests a sequence rather than a single destination: establish an entrance, follow a street, notice a change of use and return to the wider plan. Its appeal lies in the accumulated relationships of a living town. A decisive photograph of one gate can introduce that story, but it should not be allowed to stand in for the whole.

title: Sheikhupura Fort and the evidence of later occupation
summary: Sheikhupura Fort contains more than a Mughal origin story. Later residences, painted interiors and political imprisonment are integral to its architectural history.

body.text: Sheikhupura Fort is often introduced through Jahangir, but its architecture cannot be understood by stopping at a Mughal foundation. Later residential buildings, painted rooms and changes in political use are part of the site’s substance. To remove those chapters from the account would be to make the fort historically simpler than the surviving evidence allows.

The archaeological catalogue associates the main gateway and enclosure with the Mughal period while assigning much of the internal construction to later Sikh occupation. It records a residence associated with one of Ranjit Singh’s queens and floral frescoes within an upper room. The exact attribution of that room is presented cautiously in the source and should remain so. A plausible identification is not the same as an inscribed one.
An enclosure with several interiors

The fort’s outer wall establishes a strong boundary, but the buildings inside were not necessarily conceived as a single project. A useful architectural reading asks how one structure meets another. Does a wall continue uninterrupted? Has an opening been blocked? Does a staircase serve one building or link several? Such relationships can help reconstruct change without assigning every surface to a dynasty on appearance alone.

Conservation architect Saba Samee’s presentation for the Commonwealth Heritage Forum emphasises the site’s range of architectural and decorative material, including frescoes and carved timber. Her account treats the fort as a layered place spanning several periods. This is an important alternative to selecting one imagined golden moment and making all later work disappear from view.

Painted interiors are especially vulnerable to being detached from their context in public presentation. A floral panel may be beautiful, but its position within a residence helps explain how it was experienced. The room’s scale, its openings and its relation to neighbouring spaces should accompany the detail whenever possible.
Residence and confinement

The fort is also associated with the imprisonment of Maharani Jind Kaur during the nineteenth-century struggle over power in Punjab. This chapter changes the emotional register of the place. A royal building could serve as a setting for residence and later as an instrument of confinement. Those uses should not be collapsed into a picturesque story of courtly life.

It is equally important not to assign a particular surviving room as her prison without specific evidence. Historical association can be secure at the scale of a site while remaining uncertain at the scale of an individual doorway or chamber. Good interpretation explains that difference instead of manufacturing a more dramatic visitor route.

Sheikhupura Fort therefore calls for a form of conservation that preserves evidence of change. Its value is not only in the oldest masonry or the finest painted surface, but in the relationships between them. A public account that follows those relationships can show how architecture outlives its first patrons, acquires new meanings and carries histories that are not all celebratory.

title: The old Murree brewery: identifying the right ruins
summary: The old brewery ruins at Ghora Galli are not the operating Rawalpindi brewery. Keeping those sites distinct opens a clearer history of industry, water and changing production.

body.text: The name Murree Brewery can point to a company, an operating industrial site in Rawalpindi or the remains of an earlier hill complex. These are related histories, but they are not interchangeable places. The heritage record considered here concerns the old buildings at Ghora Galli. A photograph of those ruins should not be captioned as though it showed the present Rawalpindi production facilities.

The company’s own history dates establishment to 1860 and incorporation to the following year at Ghora Galli. Its environmental brochure describes later expansion into Rawalpindi and Quetta, and explains that water scarcity at the hill site contributed to a shift in brewing. By the 1920s, much of that work had moved to Rawalpindi, while malting continued at Ghora Galli into the 1940s before the property was sold.
Industry leaves more than a name

This sequence gives the ruins an industrial explanation rather than merely a colonial atmosphere. Water, production and the distribution of activities between sites matter to the story. A factory can lose one function while retaining another; the movement of brewing did not necessarily mean that every building became unused on the same day.

The Department of Archaeology and Museums describes several buildings made with dressed stone blocks and identifies extensive use of true arches. Those features provide a starting point for architectural recording. The relationship of opening, wall and roof would help explain the organisation of the complex, although the function of each surviving room cannot be assumed from appearance alone.

An industrial building is especially easy to misread once equipment has gone. A large opening might have served movement, ventilation or a production requirement, but identifying its purpose requires plans, photographs or physical evidence. Calling every substantial chamber a brewing hall would replace investigation with a plausible-sounding label.
A company archive and a physical site

Corporate history is useful primary testimony about how a company presents its development. It is not necessarily a complete account of workers, land, labour relations or the surrounding settlement. Those subjects require additional records and voices. Keeping that distinction clear prevents an industrial heritage article from becoming either advertising or an unsupported counter-history.

The company’s continuity also differs from the continuity of a particular building. A business can retain its name while changing locations, machinery and products. The hill ruins are evidence of one phase within that longer institutional history, not a frozen image of the entire enterprise.

For a heritage atlas, precise identification is therefore the first interpretive act. Place the old complex correctly, name the source of the industrial chronology and separate surviving fabric from activities documented elsewhere. The result is a more useful story than an evocative but vague account of an abandoned brewery. Current ownership, access and structural safety need separate confirmation; a catalogue entry does not make a ruined industrial site an open visitor attraction.

title: Old Badin: an archaeological city beneath a familiar name
summary: The ruins of Old Badin require a careful distinction between documented survey evidence and broad claims about antiquity. Their value does not depend on assigning them a Bronze Age origin.

body.text: Old Badin is an archaeological place-name within a district whose modern name can make the distinction easy to miss. The ruins should not be treated as a synonym for the entire present town or for every ancient site in the surrounding area. Identifying the specific recorded remains is the first step toward understanding what is known about them.

The national archaeological catalogue describes an old town in ruins and notes pressure from modern construction. It also makes a broad claim connecting the place to the Mature Harappan period. That claim needs closer scrutiny. A primary survey summary published in Pakistan Archaeology records Old Badin as site 87 and assigns it to the medieval category. The table’s key defines that category as the eighth to eighteenth centuries.
What a survey actually establishes

The 1972 report summarises a southern Sindh survey carried out by the Department of Archaeology. Its classification is evidence about the material or historical assessment available to that survey. It is not a complete excavation sequence. A medieval surface classification cannot prove that no earlier deposits exist, but neither can an unsupported statement of great antiquity establish those deposits.

This distinction gives Old Badin a useful place in a public discussion of archaeology. A settlement can be important without belonging to the earliest period a writer can name. Later towns have their own histories of occupation, production, movement and change. Adding thousands of years to an account does not make it more meaningful if the evidence has not been demonstrated.

The ruins also appear in a protected-site list reproduced in a Sindh development project’s environmental documentation. That listing confirms their recognition as a heritage concern. It does not supply a detailed plan, a foundation date or a complete account of their destruction. Different kinds of records answer different questions.
A city beneath a familiar label

For further research, the most productive starting points would be the original survey documentation, a clearly defined site boundary and dated records of visible remains. Where modern building has affected an archaeological area, knowing exactly what was observed and when becomes particularly important. A general photograph of Badin cannot substitute for that record.

Historical names may also move between an older settlement and a later town. The persistence of a name is significant, but it does not guarantee that the occupied area remained unchanged. Establishing continuity requires a combination of maps, texts and material evidence rather than a shared label alone.

Old Badin’s story is therefore still a research question, but not an empty one. There is a documented archaeological identity, a survey classification and a recognised need for protection. Presenting those securely allows future findings to refine the account. It also gives readers something valuable now: an example of how a heritage archive can distinguish evidence from repetition while taking a less celebrated urban site seriously on its own terms.

title: Mukhi Mahal and the merchant world of Hyderabad
summary: Mukhi House links Hyderabad’s domestic architecture with a later museum role. The building and its interpretation together raise questions about family memory, urban history and public access.

body.text: Mukhi House, also known as Mukhi Mahal, brings a domestic building into the public cultural life of Hyderabad. Its later museum role does not erase its earlier identity as a family residence. Instead, the two uses sit together: visitors encounter both a historic interior and a curated account of people, objects and the city around it.

The house was built around 1920–21 and is associated with Mukhi Jethanand and his family. The archaeological catalogue describes stone masonry, multiple entrances and a prominent domed element. Reporting on the museum’s opening in 2021 places the building near Pucca Qila and records displays relating to Hyderabad’s history. The small variation in published construction dates is better acknowledged than concealed behind an unjustifiably exact anniversary.
A house becomes an exhibit

In a house museum, the building is not simply a neutral container. A doorway, veranda or stair can communicate scale and hierarchy before a visitor reads a label. The route through rooms also shapes the story. An exhibition that recognises these qualities can explain domestic architecture alongside the lives represented in photographs and objects.

But the presence of an object in a historic room does not prove that it originally stood there. Interpretation should distinguish family possessions, later acquisitions and reconstructed arrangements. This makes the museum more informative, not less atmospheric. A clearly explained display allows visitors to understand which connections are documented and which are curatorial choices.

The wider story of Hyderabad’s prominent families likewise needs evidence beyond a handsome house. Architecture can demonstrate investment and ambition, but it cannot alone reconstruct a merchant’s business network or every aspect of household life. Those subjects call for correspondence, accounts, family testimony and other records, each identified for what it can contribute.
Interpretation is part of conservation

A Sindh Culture Department field report from September 2024 records instructions to provide descriptions of exhibits in Sindhi, Urdu and English. It also notes the need to coordinate major repairs to wooden structures. The two concerns belong together. A museum needs material care, but it also needs interpretation that lets different readers understand what they are seeing.

Multilingual labels should do more than translate an object’s name. A useful label can explain its date, source and relationship to the building. Where an attribution is uncertain, that uncertainty should survive translation rather than disappearing into a confident caption in one language.

Mukhi House’s significance lies in the possibility of connecting a particular home with a larger urban history without dissolving the family into an anonymous decorative past. Its architecture offers a setting; its records and collections provide the evidence for a fuller account. The museum’s current displays and visiting arrangements should be checked independently, but the essential interpretive task remains clear: allow the house, the family and Hyderabad to be seen in relationship, while preserving the distinctions between them.

title: Pucca Qila: surviving walls in an inhabited city
summary: Pucca Qila’s walls are the surviving edge of a much-altered Hyderabad fort. Its history includes royal residence, military reuse and the difficult work of conserving an inhabited urban place.

body.text: Pucca Qila is not simply a complete fort waiting to be viewed from outside. Its surviving walls enclose a place whose buildings, uses and urban relationships have changed substantially. The heritage record’s emphasis on the boundary wall is therefore meaningful: the perimeter is a major surviving part of a much more complicated historical interior.

Sindh’s Directorate General of Antiquities dates the founding of Hyderabad’s fort under Mian Ghulam Shah Kalhora to 1768. It records a further phase under Mir Fateh Ali Khan Talpur from 1789, when buildings were added for the ruling household. The same account describes extensive clearance of internal structures by the British in 1857 and subsequent military uses. These episodes explain why the enclosure cannot be read as an intact snapshot of one court.
The wall as an architectural document

The fortification’s crest carries distinctive merlons, the raised elements along the top of a defensive wall. They give the skyline a recognisable pattern, but the wall should also be examined below that outline. Changes in masonry, repaired openings and the relationship between wall and ground can reveal a different kind of history from the silhouette alone.

The provincial account identifies surviving domestic fabric associated with the Talpur period, including painted elements. Its older language judges the paintings’ taste, a judgement that need not be inherited by a modern archive. Description, attribution and condition are useful information; an unexplained dismissal of aesthetic quality is not a substitute for them.

The contrast between the strong outer boundary and the loss or alteration of internal buildings is central to the visitor’s understanding. A plan showing known historical structures and present conditions would be more informative than a reconstruction presented without explanation. It would allow absence to be understood as evidence of change rather than as an invitation to fill every gap with an imagined palace.
An urban place, not an empty stage

Conserving a fort within a living city requires attention to more than historic masonry. The surrounding streets and the people using the area are part of the present context in which any intervention occurs. A heritage account should not treat inhabitants as anonymous obstacles or imply that an attractive photograph is a sufficient measure of success.

Equally, present use does not remove the need to document and protect historic fabric. The useful discussion concerns specific conditions and responsibilities: what survives, what is vulnerable, who maintains it and how proposed work affects both buildings and people. Such questions require current evidence, not assumptions derived from the word encroachment.

A Sindh Culture Department report records a visit to Pacca Qila in September 2024, confirming continuing institutional attention without establishing the outcome of every conservation issue. The fort’s public story should maintain that same distinction between attention and completion. Pucca Qila matters because its walls frame several histories at once, and because their survival asks how an inhabited city can care for the material record within it.
